Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# Mission Control MVP v0

## Background
The customer is the operations team of an organization (org). An org can be a space agency or a private company.

Mission leads spend hours to cross-reference skill profiles, availability calendars and existing commitments. Mission staffing is the bottleneck. Mission Control finds qualified and available crew members for a mission and makes sure that they are not overloaded.

| User | Responsibility |
|------|----------------|
| Mission lead (power user) | Manages missions. Staffs them with qualified and available crew members. |
| Director | Approves or rejects missions. Oversees the org. Manages org settings (skills). |
| Crew member | Manages their profile (skills and availability). Accepts or declines assignments. |

## Requirements
### P0
P0 is the first version that is ready to pitch to a customer.

**Delivery**
1. A reviewer clones the GitHub repository and runs it locally in minutes. The repository contains setup instructions, demo seed data, this design document, the API and the CLI.
2. The repository contains evidence of verification: test output and a scripted CLI demo.
3. The seed data has 2 orgs and 2 directors in one org. It has enough crew members to show the matcher trade-offs: experts against closest fit, leave and workload.

**Auth and tenant**

4. Each org is a separate tenant with exclusive data access. The data-access layer and composite foreign keys enforce this.
5. Each user has one role: director, lead or crew member. The API enforces the role permissions.
6. A user logs in to the CLI as a seeded user (`mc login --user username`).
7. For a forbidden action, the CLI shows a clear error with the role and the rule.

**Mission lifecycle**

8. Each mission needs approval. The lead submits the mission to a director.
9. The director approves or rejects the mission. The approval view shows the matcher preview.
10. Crew members accept or decline assignments.
11. Directors see the whole org: all missions and all crew members (API and CLI).

**Crew and skills**

12. Crew members manage their skill profile via the CLI. They list, add, update and remove their own skills from the org catalogue, with a proficiency level.
13. Crew members manage their availability via the CLI. They list, add and remove their own unavailability.
14. Crew members see their own assignments with history (past, declined), their profile and the mission details. They accept or decline assignments.
15. Each org has its own set of skills. P0 seeds the skills. P1 adds skill editing.

**Matching**

16. The matcher suggests crew members for a mission. The inputs are skills, availability and workload.
17. The lead runs a read-only matcher preview in DRAFT to check that the mission can be staffed.
18. The lead invites crew members only when the mission is APPROVED.
19. Rematching fills only open slots. It never suggests a crew member who declined this mission.

**CLI**

20. The primary workflows run through the CLI. See [CLI](#cli).

**Quality**

21. Tests cover the happy path per workflow: lifecycle, matcher, invites and responses, crew profile.
22. Cross-org access checks make sure that resources of another org return 404.
23. A scripted end-to-end CLI demo runs the full mission lifecycle over the seed data.

#### Build order
Each step ends with its happy path test and its cross-org check. Each step is one or more commits.

1. Skeleton: docker-compose Postgres, FastAPI app, Alembic, Typer entry point, README run steps.
2. Data model, first migration and seed data: 2 orgs, 2 directors in one org, leads, crew, skills, leave, existing assignments for workload.
3. Auth and tenant: `mc login`, JWT with `user_id`, per-request load of user, org and role, org-scoped data-access layer, RBAC error format.
4. Missions in DRAFT: create, edit, slots, list, show.
5. Matcher preview: filters, ranking, slot assignment. `mc missions match`.
6. Approval: submit, withdraw, approve, reject. No self approval, additional director flag, matcher preview in the approval view.
7. Staffing: invite, `mc assignments list / accept / decline`, double booking check, decliner exclusion on rematch.
8. Remaining transitions: withdraw from APPROVED to DRAFT, start (with guard), complete, cancel. Assignment cancellation.
9. Crew profile: `mc profile show`, skills, availability.
10. Org crew view: directors and leads list and show the crew members of the org (requirement 11). Leads see leave as "unavailable" without the reason.
11. Scripted end-to-end CLI demo and test results in the README.

### P1
P1 extends the MVP if time permits in this session.

1. Directors manage the org skill catalogue.
2. Mission audit logs.
3. Decision insights for the lead: why the matcher excluded a crew member.
4. Rank breakdown per suggestion: why a crew member is the best fit for the slot.
5. Short references for missions (`MSN-<n>`) and skills (`slug`) in the CLI. See [Short references](#short-references).

P2 is out of scope for this session.

| Area | Item |
|------|------|
| Auth and tenant | Noisy-neighbour protection and uneven org sizes |
| | Real IdP (OIDC), login and signup |
| | Postgres RLS as a second layer for reads |

| | Reassign the lead of a mission |
| Crew and skills | Edit and archive skills |
| | Verification of self-assessed proficiency |
| Matching | Additional resource constraints |
| | Report of skill gaps and possible resolutions when no match exists |
| | Rest buffer between missions |
| | Mission priority |
| | Optimization for large orgs |
| Operations | CI/CD |
| | Scalability, observability, IaC, offline jobs |

## Tech stack
The API and the CLI use one language (Python). This keeps the stack small.

| Component | Choice | Reason |
|-----------|--------|--------|
| CLI | Typer, httpx, Rich | Typed commands, generated help, readable tables. The CLI calls the API and stores the token locally after login. |
| API | FastAPI, Pydantic | Typed API with generated OpenAPI docs. |
| Data access | SQLAlchemy, Alembic | Safe DB access with migrations. |
| Database | Postgres | |

# Mission Control

Mission Control finds qualified and available crew members for a mission. It is a multi-tenant API with a CLI (`mc`).

- Design: [design/DESIGN.md](design/DESIGN.md)
- Challenge brief: [BRIEF.md](BRIEF.md)

## Prerequisites
- Docker with Compose
- [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). uv installs Python 3.12 if necessary.

## Run locally
```sh
docker compose up -d                       # Postgres on localhost:5432
uv sync                                    # install the workspace into .venv
uv run alembic upgrade head                # apply DB migrations
uv run mc-seed                             # load the demo data
uv run uvicorn mc_api.main:app --reload    # API on http://localhost:8000
```

In a second terminal:
```sh
uv run mc health                           # API ok, database ok
uv run mc login --user diana               # store a token
uv run mc whoami                           # show the user, the role and the org
uv run mc --help
```

The token is in `~/.config/mc/token`. `MC_CONFIG_DIR` overrides the folder. `mc logout` deletes the token.

The API docs are at http://localhost:8000/docs.

## Test
Postgres must run (`docker compose up -d`). The tests use the database `mc_test`. The test run creates it.
```sh
uv run pytest
```

## Seed data
`mc-seed` loads a fixed demo dataset: 2 orgs, 20 users, skills, leave, 5 missions and their assignments.

**Warning:** `mc-seed` deletes all data in the database of `DATABASE_URL`. Use it only on a local demo database.

# Mission Control

Mission Control finds qualified and available crew members for a mission. It is a multi-tenant API with a CLI (`mc`).

- Design: [design/DESIGN.md](design/DESIGN.md)
- Challenge brief: [BRIEF.md](BRIEF.md)

## Prerequisites
- Docker with Compose
- [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). uv installs Python 3.12 if necessary.

## Run locally
```sh
docker compose up -d                       # Postgres on localhost:5432
uv sync                                    # install the workspace into .venv
uv run alembic upgrade head                # apply DB migrations
uv run mc-seed                             # load the demo data
uv run uvicorn mc_api.main:app --reload    # API on http://localhost:8000
```

In a second terminal:
```sh
uv run mc health                           # API ok, database ok
uv run mc login --user diana               # store a token
uv run mc whoami                           # show the user, the role and the org
uv run mc --help
```

The token is in `~/.config/mc/token`. `MC_CONFIG_DIR` overrides the folder. `mc logout` deletes the token.

The API docs are at http://localhost:8000/docs.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Checks for the verify tiers (D4). Usage: check.sh fast|full
# Prints only failures, each line marked ERROR. Exits non-zero if a check fails.
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1
failed=0

# Runs one check: run <name> '<command>'. On failure, prints the last 40 lines (a build log can have hundreds).
# Give one command for each call. A chain prints the success output of the earlier commands when a later one fails.
run() {
  local name=$1 out
  shift
  out=$(bash -c "$*" 2>&1) || { tail -n 40 <<<"$out" | sed "s/^/ERROR: $name: /"; failed=1; }
}

# Format check, lint, typecheck and unit tests. Example: run api-lint 'cd api && uv run ruff check .'
fast() {
  run format 'uv run ruff format --check -q .'
  run lint 'uv run ruff check -q .'
  run tests 'uv run pytest -q -m "not e2e"'
}

# Build, all other tests and e2e. Give each e2e step its own call: start, smoke, browser tests, stop.
full() {
  run e2e 'uv run pytest -q -m e2e'
}

case "${1:-}" in
  fast) fast ;;
  full) fast; full ;;
  *) echo "ERROR: Unknown tier. Use: check.sh fast|full" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
exit "$failed"
# Project values for the kit hooks. Copy to .claude/project.sh. The hooks source it. Do not run it.
# Give one line for each area, with a comment that names the area and its tool.

# Test files: extended regexes on repo-relative paths. The test lock blocks edits to each match.
# Include test setup and e2e files. If the agent can change them, a test can pass without a fix.
TEST_PATTERNS=(
  '^packages/[^/]+/tests/'   # all packages: pytest
)

# Formats one file after each edit. $1 is the repo-relative path. It runs at the repo root.
# Delete this function if the project has no formatter.
format() {
  case "$1" in
    *.py) uv run ruff format -q "$1" && uv run ruff check --fix -q "$1" ;;
  esac
}

Base directory for this skill: /Users/janeshorst/.claude-mutinex/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.4.1/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

## Establish Shared Understanding

The outcome of brainstorming is an understanding your human partner can
recognize and correct, grounded in what they want to accomplish.

1. **Discover intent.** Use the request and available context to identify
   the intended outcome, who it is for, and what success looks like. When
   that information is missing, ask one focused question about purpose or
   intended use before proposing features or an approach. Knowing the app
   genre does not tell you why your partner wants it. Gathering missing
   requirements does not ask them to authorize the task again.
2. **Write back your understanding.** Summarize the intended outcome,
   relevant constraints, and success criteria in a short note your partner
   can assess. Separate what they said from assumptions. Invite correction
   and incorporate their answer before treating this as the design brief.
3. **Carry intent into the design.** Preserve the agreed understanding in
   the selected path's design artifact: the written spec for architectural
   work, or the in-chat design/probe for bounded work and spikes. Check
   proposed features and technical choices against that understanding.

When the request already supplies the purpose and constraints, reflect
that understanding instead of asking the same questions again. Keep the
note concise; its accuracy and the opportunity to correct it matter.

<HARD-GATE>
Before taking any implementation action, including invoking an
implementation skill, writing product code, scaffolding, installing
product dependencies, or creating an external project, complete the
selected path's prerequisites:

- Spike: the human partner approves the question and probe.
- Bounded: the human partner approves the short in-chat design.
- Architectural: the human partner reviews and approves the written spec,
  then reviews the written implementation plan and selects its execution
  method. Conversational design approval only permits writing the spec;
  written-spec approval only permits invoking writing-plans.

A reply approves the stage actually presented. Approval of an idea or
feature scope does not approve artifacts that do not exist yet. Resume
at the earliest incomplete stage; do not turn one approval into permission
to skip the rest of the selected path. Read-only project exploration is
allowed while those prerequisites remain incomplete.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving the required design
before implementation. A bounded change may need only two sentences in
chat. A new todo-list project is architectural and requires the written
spec and planning handoffs. Scale the artifact to the selected path;
complete that path's reviews before implementation.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Follow the selected path: a bounded change gets a short chat design; an architectural change gets the written spec and planning handoffs. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];

    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

# Spec: staffing

## Goal
Add staffing for APPROVED missions in the API and the CLI (build step 7, `design/DESIGN.md:70`). The mission lead invites crew members to open slots. Crew members list, accept and decline their assignments. The API blocks double booking, unqualified crew members, crew members on leave and decliners of the mission (DESIGN req 10, 14, 18). The lead runs the matcher preview on an APPROVED mission to fill the open slots again (DESIGN req 19).

## Acceptance criteria
All dates in the examples use the mission 2027-03-01 to 2027-03-10, unless the example gives other dates. All date ranges include both end dates (`design/DESIGN.md:183`).

| ID | Criterion | The tests must prove |
|---|---|---|
| AC1 | The lead of an APPROVED mission invites a crew member to an open slot (DESIGN 18, 290, 330). | `POST /missions/{id}/assignments` with `{"position": 2, "username": "<crew>"}` by the mission lead gives 201 and a `MissionOut`. Slot 2 has `crew_username` = the crew member and `assignment_status` = `INVITED`. The DB has one new assignment row with status INVITED and `responded_at` null. This is true for a lead and for a director who leads the mission. |
| AC2 | Only the lead of the mission invites (DESIGN 324). | Another lead and a director of the own org each get 403. The body is `{"role": "<ROLE>", "rule": "Directors and leads invite crew only to their own missions"}`. No row is added. |
| AC3 | Crew members cannot invite (DESIGN 330). | A crew member gets 403. The body is `{"role": "CREW", "rule": "Only directors and leads manage and view missions"}`. |
| AC4 | The invite is allowed only in APPROVED (DESIGN 18, 299). | For a mission in each other status, the lead gets 409. The body is `{"detail": "Mission is <STATUS>. Invites are allowed only in APPROVED."}`. |
| AC5 | A mission of another org is not visible (DESIGN req 4, 22). | A lead and a director of org A each get 404 for an invite to a mission of org B. Each body equals the body for a random UUID: `{"detail": "Not found"}`. |
| AC6 | The invite names an active slot (DESIGN 216). | A position with no slot, or a position of an archived slot only, gives 422 with `{"detail": "Unknown slot: <N>"}`. |
| AC7 | The invite names a crew member of the own org (DESIGN 345, 356). | A username that does not exist gives 422 with `{"detail": "Unknown crew member: <username>"}`. A username of a crew member of org B gives the same status and the same body. A lead or a director of the own org gives 422 with `{"detail": "<username> is not a crew member. Only crew members can be assigned to missions."}`. |
| AC8 | A slot has a maximum of one INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment (DESIGN 232). | A slot with an INVITED or an ACCEPTED assignment gives 409 with `{"detail": "Slot <N> already has an INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment."}`. A slot with only DECLINED or CANCELLED assignments accepts a new invite. |
| AC9 | A crew member fills a maximum of one slot of a mission (DESIGN 231, 282). | A crew member with an INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment on slot 1 gives 409 for an invite to slot 2: `{"detail": "<username> already has an INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment on this mission."}`. |
| AC10 | The lead cannot invite a crew member who declined this mission (DESIGN 19, 301). | A crew member with a DECLINED assignment on any slot of this mission gives 409 with `{"detail": "<username> declined this mission."}`. A crew member with only a CANCELLED assignment on this mission can be invited. |
| AC11 | The invited crew member has the slot skill at the minimum level or higher (DESIGN 393). | Slot EVA ≥ 3. EVA 3 → 201. EVA 2 → 409. No EVA → 409. The 409 body is `{"detail": "<username> does not have EVA at level 3 or higher."}`. |
| AC12 | The invited crew member has no unavailability in the mission dates. The message does not show the reason (DESIGN 184, 394). | Leave that ends on 2027-03-01 or starts on 2027-03-10 → 409 with `{"detail": "<username> is unavailable from <start> to <end>."}`, with the dates of the leave. If more leave entries overlap, the message names the one with the earliest start. The body does not contain the reason. Leave that ends on 2027-02-28 or starts on 2027-03-11 → 201. |
| AC13 | The invite rejects double booking: an INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment on another mission with overlapping dates (DESIGN 304). | An INVITED or an ACCEPTED assignment on a mission from 2027-03-10 to 2027-03-15 → 409 with `{"detail": "<username> is booked on mission \"<title>\" from 2027-03-10 to 2027-03-15."}`. A DECLINED or CANCELLED assignment on that mission → 201. An ACCEPTED assignment on a mission that ends on 2027-02-28 → 201. If more missions overlap, the message names the one with the earliest start. |
| AC14 | The invite locks the crew user row before the double booking check (DESIGN 304). | Integration, committed data, two DB connections. Connection X locks the crew user row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. An invite of that crew member starts in a second thread and does not complete within 0.5 s. X adds an INVITED assignment on an overlapping mission and commits. The invite then completes with 409. |
| AC15 | A crew member lists the own assignments with history (DESIGN 14, 334, 429). | `GET /assignments` by a crew member gives 200 and all own assignments in each status. Each entry has `id`, `mission_id`, `mission_title`, `mission_status`, `start_date`, `end_date`, `lead_username`, `position`, `skill_name`, `min_level`, `status` and `responded_at`. The order is mission `start_date` descending, then `position`. Assignments of other crew members of the own org are not in the list. A crew member with no assignment gets `[]`. |
| AC16 | Only crew members list and respond to assignments (DESIGN 334-335). | A lead and a director each get 403 for `GET /assignments`, `POST /assignments/{id}/accept` and `POST /assignments/{id}/decline`. The body is `{"role": "<ROLE>", "rule": "Only crew members view and respond to assignments"}`. |
| AC17 | A crew member accepts an INVITED assignment (DESIGN 291). | `POST /assignments/{mission_id}/accept` gives 200 and the `AssignmentOut` with status ACCEPTED and `responded_at` set. The DB row has the same values. |
| AC18 | A crew member declines an INVITED assignment. The slot is open again (DESIGN 292, 301). | `POST /assignments/{mission_id}/decline` gives 200 and the `AssignmentOut` with status DECLINED and `responded_at` set. After the decline, the lead invites another qualified crew member to the same slot → 201. |
| AC19 | Only an INVITED assignment can be accepted or declined (DESIGN 291-292, P2 at DESIGN 95). | A crew member with only ACCEPTED, DECLINED or CANCELLED assignments on the mission gets 409 for accept and for decline: `{"detail": "You have no open invite for this mission."}`. The row does not change. |
| AC20 | A crew member responds only on a mission with an own assignment. Another org stays hidden (DESIGN req 4, 22; DESIGN 334). | A mission of the own org with no assignment of the crew member gives 404. A mission of org B gives 404. A random UUID gives 404. All three bodies are `{"detail": "Not found"}`. |
| AC21 | Accept rejects double booking with another mission (DESIGN 304). | Mission M, 2027-03-01 to 2027-03-10, has an INVITED assignment of the crew member. Another mission from 2027-03-05 to 2027-03-06 has an ACCEPTED assignment of the crew member. The test adds this row directly in the DB. Accept on M → 409 with `{"detail": "You are booked on mission \"<title>\" from 2027-03-05 to 2027-03-06."}`. The INVITED row of M does not change. Accept does not check the skill level or the leave again. |
| AC22 | Accept locks the crew user row before the double booking check (DESIGN 304). | Integration, committed data, as AC14. Connection X locks the crew user row. Accept starts in a second thread and does not complete within 0.5 s. X adds an ACCEPTED assignment on an overlapping mission and commits. Accept then completes with 409. |
| AC23 | The mission view shows the staffing progress of each slot (DESIGN 279). | `GET /missions/{id}` gives each slot `crew_username` and `assignment_status` of its INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment. A slot with no such assignment, or with only DECLINED or CANCELLED assignments, has `null` for both. `mc missions show` has the columns Slot, Skill, Min level, Crew, Status. An open slot has empty Crew and Status cells. |
| AC24 | `mc missions invite <mission-id> --slot N --crew <username>` invites (DESIGN 428). | Exit 0 and the mission output with the new Crew and Status in the slot row. An API error prints the message of the existing error format and exits 1. |
| AC25 | `mc assignments list` shows the own assignments (DESIGN 429). | The table has the columns Mission ID, Title, Start, End, Slot, Skill, Status, Responded. The Mission ID column is not wrapped. A `null` `responded_at` gives an empty Responded cell. Exit 0. |
| AC26 | `mc assignments accept <mission-id>` and `mc assignments decline <mission-id>` respond (DESIGN 430). | Exit 0. The output contains the mission title and the new status `ACCEPTED` or `DECLINED`. An API error prints the message and exits 1. |
| AC27 | Each state change and each rejection in the new API code writes an info log line. The line contains no token (CLAUDE.md conventions). | A log check with `caplog` for one invite, one accept, one decline and one rejected invite. Each gives one or more INFO records of a logger under `mc_api.`. |
| AC28 | The docs describe staffing and rematch as built. | `design/DESIGN.md` build step 7 does not change. The "Assignment states" section lists the invite checks of AC6 to AC13 in the check order, the rule for more than one conflict, and the accept check of AC21. The permission row "Run the matcher on own missions" reads "(preview in DRAFT and APPROVED)". The rule "Rematching fills only open slots" exists in "Slot assignment" and does not change. |
| AC29 | The lead runs the matcher preview on an APPROVED mission. The preview lists only open slots and never suggests a decliner of the mission (DESIGN req 19, 301). | APPROVED mission: slot 1 has an ACCEPTED assignment of `a`. Slot 2 has a DECLINED assignment of `b`, who has the closest skill level. `c` is qualified and free. `GET /missions/{id}/match` by the lead gives 200 with only slot 2, and the suggestion `c`. A DRAFT mission with no assignments gives the same result as before this step. |
| AC30 | The matcher preview is allowed only in DRAFT and APPROVED. | For a mission in APPROVAL_REQUIRED, ACTIVE, COMPLETED or CANCELLED, the lead gets 409 with `{"detail": "Mission is <STATUS>. The matcher preview is allowed only in DRAFT and APPROVED."}`. |

## Non-goals
- A change of the matcher filters, ranking or solver (step 5). The filters already exclude decliners, leave and double booking (`packages/api/src/mc_api/routers/missions.py:345-381`).
- The approval transitions (step 6), and the matcher preview in the approval view for directors (DESIGN req 9).
- Assignment cancellation when the mission goes back to DRAFT or is cancelled (step 8).
- A change of the profile conflict checks for skills and leave. They exist on `develop` (`packages/api/src/mc_api/routers/profile.py:101-188`).
- A separate mission detail command or route for crew members. `AssignmentOut` carries the mission details.
- Withdraw or decline after accept (P2, `design/DESIGN.md:95`).
- A README change. `README.md` lists no mission commands. The demo step (step 11) adds the CLI commands.
- A seed change. The E2E test does not cover the double booking check. Integration tests cover it.
- A schema change or a migration. The `assignment` table and its partial unique indexes exist (`packages/api/src/mc_api/models.py:163-197`).
- Notifications to crew members.

## End-to-end check
The E2E test uses the seed data and uvicorn on a free port, as the step 4 E2E test does (`packages/api/tests/e2e/conftest.py:17-45`). The CLI gets each mission ID from `mc missions list` or `mc assignments list`.

| 4 | `mc login --user hana`, `mc assignments list`, `mc assignments decline <id of "Orbital Debris Survey">` | The list has "Orbital Debris Survey" with `INVITED` and "Lunar Relay Repair" with `DECLINED`. Decline exits 0 and shows `DECLINED`. | `packages/api/tests/e2e/test_staffing_cli.py` |

@app.command()
def create(
    title: str = typer.Option(..., "--title"),
    start: str = typer.Option(..., "--start", help="Start date, YYYY-MM-DD."),
    end: str = typer.Option(..., "--end", help="End date, YYYY-MM-DD."),
    description: str | None = typer.Option(None, "--description"),
) -> None:
    """Create a DRAFT mission that you lead."""
    # Dates go as text, so the API checks them.
    body = {"title": title, "start_date": start, "end_date": end, "description": description}
    mission = MissionOut.model_validate(request("POST", "/missions", json=body).json())
    console.print(f"Created mission {mission.id}")
    print_mission(mission)


@app.command("list")
def list_missions() -> None:
    """List the missions of your org."""
    table = Table("ID", "Title", "Status", "Start", "End", "Lead")
    table.columns[0].no_wrap = True
    for item in request("GET", "/missions").json():
        m = MissionSummary.model_validate(item)
        table.add_row(
            str(m.id), m.title, m.status, str(m.start_date), str(m.end_date), m.lead_username
        )
    console.print(table)


@app.command()
def show(mission_id: str) -> None:
    """Show a mission and its slots."""
    print_mission(
        MissionOut.model_validate(request("GET", f"/missions/{quote(mission_id, safe='')}").json())
    )


@app.command()
def match(mission_id: str) -> None:
    """Show the closest-fit crew member for each slot of a DRAFT mission that you lead."""
    path = f"/missions/{quote(mission_id, safe='')}/match"
    preview = MatchPreview.model_validate(request("GET", path).json())
    table = Table("Slot", "Skill", "Min level", "Crew", "Level", "Workload days")
    for m in preview.slots:
        s, c = m.slot, m.suggestion
        table.add_row(
            str(s.position),
            s.skill_name,
            str(s.min_level),
            c.username if c else "No match",
            str(c.level) if c else "",
            str(c.workload_days) if c else "",
        )
    console.print(table)
    filled = sum(m.suggestion is not None for m in preview.slots)
    console.print(f"{filled} of {len(preview.slots)} slots filled")


@app.command()
def edit(
    mission_id: str,
    title: str | None = typer.Option(None, "--title"),
    description: str | None = typer.Option(None, "--description"),
    start: str | None = typer.Option(None, "--start", help="Start date, YYYY-MM-DD."),
    end: str | None = typer.Option(None, "--end", help="End date, YYYY-MM-DD."),
) -> None:
    """Edit a DRAFT mission that you lead. Only the given options change."""
    given = {"title": title, "description": description, "start_date": start, "end_date": end}
    body = {k: v for k, v in given.items() if v is not None}
    path = f"/missions/{quote(mission_id, safe='')}"
    print_mission(MissionOut.model_validate(request("PATCH", path, json=body).json()))


@app.command()
def submit(mission_id: str) -> None:
    """Submit a DRAFT mission that you lead for approval."""
    path = f"/missions/{quote(mission_id, safe='')}/submit"
    print_mission(MissionOut.model_validate(request("POST", path).json()))


@app.command()
def withdraw(mission_id: str) -> None:
    """Withdraw a mission that you lead from APPROVAL_REQUIRED to DRAFT."""
    path = f"/missions/{quote(mission_id, safe='')}/withdraw"
    print_mission(MissionOut.model_validate(request("POST", path).json()))


@app.command()
def invite(
    mission_id: str,
    slot: int = typer.Option(..., "--slot", help="Slot number."),
    crew: str = typer.Option(..., "--crew", help="Username of the crew member."),
) -> None:
    """Invite a crew member to an open slot of an APPROVED mission that you lead."""
    path = f"/missions/{quote(mission_id, safe='')}/assignments"
    body = {"position": slot, "username": crew}
    print_mission(MissionOut.model_validate(request("POST", path, json=body).json()))


@app.command()
def approve(mission_id: str) -> None:
    """Approve an APPROVAL_REQUIRED mission that you do not lead (directors only)."""
    path = f"/missions/{quote(mission_id, safe='')}/approve"
    print_mission(MissionOut.model_validate(request("POST", path).json()))


@app.command()
def reject(mission_id: str) -> None:
    """Reject an APPROVAL_REQUIRED mission that you do not lead and return it to DRAFT."""
    path = f"/missions/{quote(mission_id, safe='')}/reject"
    print_mission(MissionOut.model_validate(request("POST", path).json()))

## Matching engine
The matcher fills each slot with one crew member. A slot is one skill with a minimum level.

### Filters
The matcher includes a crew member in the selection set only if all conditions are true:
- The crew member is in the same org.
- The crew member has the skill at the minimum level or higher.
- The crew member has no unavailability, INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment in the mission timeframe.
- The crew member has not declined this mission.

### Ranking
The matcher ranks the candidates of a slot in this strict order. A later rule applies only at a full tie of the earlier rules.
1. **Proficiency is closest to the minimum (gap).** The gap is `level - min_level`. Experts stay free for missions with higher proficiency requirements.
2. **Scarcity is lower.** Scarcity is the max of `1 / holders` over the other skills of the crew member, without the slot skill. `holders` counts the CREW members of the org with the skill at any level. A crew member with no other skill has scarcity 0. The matcher keeps the holders of a rare skill free.
3. **Workload is lower.** Workload is the number of booked mission days (INVITED and ACCEPTED) in a window of 90 days before and after the mission. Workload is only a tie breaker. A workload cap is P2.
4. **The username is first in alphabetical order.** This rule makes each result deterministic.

### Slot assignment
- The matcher assigns all slots together, not one by one.
- scipy `linear_sum_assignment` solves a slots x candidates cost matrix. A big cost marks the ineligible pairs, so the solver fills the maximum number of slots first.
- Rematching fills only open slots. An open slot has no INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment.

### Availability
Crew members manage unavailable time slots, not available periods. Examples are holiday leave, sick leave and internal meetings. The time slots use dates only.

The matcher ranks the candidates of a slot in this strict order. A later rule applies only at a full tie of the earlier rules.
1. **Proficiency is closest to the minimum (gap).** The gap is `level - min_level`. Experts stay free for missions with higher proficiency requirements.
2. **Scarcity is lower.** Scarcity is the max of `1 / holders` over the other skills of the crew member, without the slot skill. `holders` counts the CREW members of the org with the skill at any level. A crew member with no other skill has scarcity 0. The matcher keeps the holders of a rare skill free.
3. **Workload is lower.** Workload is the number of booked mission days (INVITED and ACCEPTED) in a window of 90 days before and after the mission. Workload is only a tie breaker. A workload cap is P2.
4. **The username is first in alphabetical order.** This rule makes each result deterministic.

### Slot assignment
- The matcher assigns all slots together, not one by one.
- scipy `linear_sum_assignment` solves a slots x candidates cost matrix. A big cost marks the ineligible pairs, so the solver fills the maximum number of slots first.
- Rematching fills only open slots. An open slot has no INVITED or ACCEPTED assignment.

### Availability
Crew members manage unavailable time slots, not available periods. Examples are holiday leave, sick leave and internal meetings. The time slots use dates only.

# Spec: readme-demo

## Goal
Add a scripted end-to-end CLI demo and test results to the README (build step 11, `design/DESIGN.md:74`). The demo runs the mission lifecycle from create to accept over the seed data. An E2E test runs the script, so `verify:full` catches regressions. This gives a reviewer evidence of verification (DESIGN req 2, 23). Steps 8 and 10 move to P1.

## Precondition
Build step 7 (staffing) is finished and committed. It adds `mc missions invite`, `mc assignments list|accept|decline` and the matcher preview on APPROVED missions (`.work/staffing/spec.md`, AC24 to AC30). The demo uses these commands.

## Acceptance criteria
The demo mission is "Demo Survey", 2027-03-01 to 2027-03-10. It has slot 1 Piloting level 3 and slot 2 Medicine level 3. The seed data has no booking or leave of ben, hana or fay in these dates (`packages/api/src/mc_api/seed.py`). Ben and hana have the closest fit by the ranking at `design/DESIGN.md:398`.

| ID | Criterion | The tests must prove |
|---|---|---|
| AC1 | `scripts/demo.sh` resets the data with `uv run mc-seed`, then runs the journey (DESIGN req 23). | The script exits 0 on a clean database. It exits 0 again on a second run. The output has one heading line for each journey step. |
| AC2 | Leo creates the mission, adds the two slots and runs the matcher preview in DRAFT (DESIGN req 17). | The preview output has slot 1 `ben` and slot 2 `hana`, and `2 of 2 slots filled`. |

| AC4 | Leo invites ben to slot 1 and hana to slot 2 (DESIGN req 18). Ben accepts. Hana declines (DESIGN req 10). | After the invites, the mission output has `ben` `INVITED` and `hana` `INVITED`. The accept output has `ACCEPTED`. The decline output has `DECLINED`. |
| AC5 | Leo runs the matcher preview on the APPROVED mission. The preview fills only the open slot and does not suggest hana (DESIGN req 19). Leo invites fay. Fay accepts. | The preview has one row: slot 2, `fay`. It does not contain `hana`. After the last accept, `mc missions show` has `ben` `ACCEPTED` and `fay` `ACCEPTED`. |
| AC6 | The demo shows a forbidden action with the role and the rule (DESIGN req 7). | Ava (CREW) runs `mc missions invite`. The step exits 1 in the script and the output has `CREW` and `Only directors and leads manage and view missions`. The script continues. |
| AC7 | The demo shows a cross-org check (DESIGN req 22). | Nick (lead of the other org) runs `mc missions show <Demo Survey id>`. The output has `Not found`. The script continues. |

from urllib.parse import quote

import typer
from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

from mc_cli.client import request
from mc_shared import CrewSkillOut, ProfileOut, UnavailabilityOut

app = typer.Typer()
console = Console(markup=False, highlight=False, emoji=False)


@app.command()
def show() -> None:
    """Show your profile."""
    profile = ProfileOut.model_validate(request("GET", "/profile").json())
    console.print(f"{profile.username} ({profile.display_name}), org {profile.org_name}")


skills = typer.Typer()
app.add_typer(skills, name="skills", help="List, set and remove your skills.")


@skills.command("list")
def list_skills() -> None:
    """List your skills."""
    table = Table("Skill ID", "Skill", "Level")
    table.columns[0].no_wrap = True
    for item in request("GET", "/profile/skills").json():
        s = CrewSkillOut.model_validate(item)
        table.add_row(str(s.skill_id), s.skill_name, str(s.level))
    console.print(table)


@skills.command("set")
def set_skill(skill_id: str, level: int = typer.Option(..., "--level")) -> None:
    """Add a skill or change its level."""
    path = f"/profile/skills/{quote(skill_id, safe='')}"
    s = CrewSkillOut.model_validate(request("PUT", path, json={"level": level}).json())
    console.print(f"Set {s.skill_name} to level {s.level}")


@skills.command()
def remove(skill_id: str) -> None:
    """Remove a skill from your profile."""
    request("DELETE", f"/profile/skills/{quote(skill_id, safe='')}")
    console.print(f"Removed skill {skill_id}")


availability = typer.Typer()
app.add_typer(availability, name="availability", help="List, add and remove your unavailability.")


@availability.command("list")
def list_availability() -> None:
    """List your unavailability."""
    table = Table("ID", "From", "To", "Reason")
    table.columns[0].no_wrap = True
    for item in request("GET", "/profile/unavailability").json():
        u = UnavailabilityOut.model_validate(item)
        table.add_row(str(u.id), str(u.start_date), str(u.end_date), str(u.reason))
    console.print(table)


@availability.command("add")
def add_availability(
    start: str = typer.Option(..., "--from", help="First day, YYYY-MM-DD."),
    end: str = typer.Option(..., "--to", help="Last day, YYYY-MM-DD."),
    reason: str = typer.Option(..., "--reason", help="HOLIDAY, SICK or MEETING."),
) -> None:
    """Add a period when you are unavailable."""
    body = {"start_date": start, "end_date": end, "reason": reason}
    u = UnavailabilityOut.model_validate(
        request("POST", "/profile/unavailability", json=body).json()
    )
    console.print(f"Added unavailability {u.id}")


@availability.command("remove")
def remove_availability(unavailability_id: str) -> None:
    """Remove one of your unavailability entries."""
    request("DELETE", f"/profile/unavailability/{quote(unavailability_id, safe='')}")
    console.print(f"Removed unavailability {unavailability_id}")
import re

import pytest
from test_missions_cli import skill_ids

pytestmark = pytest.mark.e2e

    assert mc("login", "--user", "ava")[0] == 0

    code, out = mc("profile", "show")
    assert code == 0
    assert all(word in out for word in ("ava", "Ava Lindqvist", "Artemis Space Agency"))

    # Spec steps 2 to 4: list, set and remove skills.
    ids = skill_ids(mc("skills", "list")[1])
    code, out = mc("profile", "skills", "list")
    assert code == 0
    assert re.search(r"Piloting\W+5", out) and re.search(r"Communications\W+4", out)

    code, out = mc("profile", "skills", "set", ids["EVA"], "--level", "2")
    assert code == 0
    assert "Set EVA to level 2" in out
    code, out = mc("profile", "skills", "set", ids["Piloting"], "--level", "4")
    assert code == 0
    assert "Set Piloting to level 4" in out
    out = mc("profile", "skills", "list")[1]
    assert re.search(r"EVA\W+2", out) and re.search(r"Piloting\W+4", out)

    code, out = mc("profile", "skills", "remove", ids["EVA"])
    assert code == 0
    assert f"Removed skill {ids['EVA']}" in out
    assert "EVA" not in mc("profile", "skills", "list")[1]

    code, out = mc("profile", "skills", "remove", "abc")
    assert code == 1
    assert "Traceback" not in out

    # Spec steps 5 and 6: add, list and remove unavailability.
    code, out = mc(

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

# Spec: readme-demo

## Goal
Add a scripted end-to-end CLI demo and test results to the README (build step 11, `design/DESIGN.md:74`). The demo shows a crew member who manages the own profile. It then runs the mission lifecycle from create to accept over the seed data. An E2E test runs the script, so `verify:full` catches regressions. This gives a reviewer evidence of verification (DESIGN req 2, 23). Steps 8 and 10 move to P1.

## Precondition
Build step 7 (staffing) is finished and committed. It adds `mc missions invite`, `mc assignments list|accept|decline` and the matcher preview on APPROVED missions (`.work/staffing/spec.md`, AC24 to AC30). The demo uses these commands.

## Acceptance criteria
The demo mission is "Demo Survey", 2027-03-01 to 2027-03-10. It has slot 1 Piloting level 3 and slot 2 Medicine level 3. The seed data has no booking or leave of ben, hana or fay in these dates (`packages/api/src/mc_api/seed.py`). Ben and hana have the closest fit by the ranking at `design/DESIGN.md:398`. The profile step changes only the Geology level of ben and a leave in June 2027. Neither change affects the matcher result.

| ID | Criterion | The tests must prove |
|---|---|---|
| AC1 | `scripts/demo.sh` resets the data with `uv run mc-seed`, then runs the journey (DESIGN req 23). | The script exits 0 on a clean database. It exits 0 again on a second run. The output has one heading line for each journey step. |
| AC2 | Ben manages the own profile (DESIGN req 12, 13). Ben shows the profile, sets Geology to level 3, and lists the skills. Ben adds leave from 2027-06-01 to 2027-06-03, lists it, and removes it. | The profile output has `ben`, `Ben Carter` and `Artemis Space Agency`. The skill list has Geology with level 3. The add output has `Added unavailability <id>`. The list has the entry with `HOLIDAY`. After the remove, the list does not have the id. |
| AC3 | Leo creates the mission, adds the two slots and runs the matcher preview in DRAFT (DESIGN req 17). | The preview output has slot 1 `ben` and slot 2 `hana`, and `2 of 2 slots filled`. |
| AC4 | Leo submits. Diana approves (DESIGN req 8, 9). | The submit output shows `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`. The approve output shows `APPROVED`. |
| AC5 | Leo invites ben to slot 1 and hana to slot 2 (DESIGN req 18). Ben accepts. Hana declines (DESIGN req 10, 14). | After the invites, the mission output has `ben` `INVITED` and `hana` `INVITED`. The accept output has `ACCEPTED`. The decline output has `DECLINED`. |
| AC6 | Leo runs the matcher preview on the APPROVED mission. The preview fills only the open slot and does not suggest hana (DESIGN req 19). Leo invites fay. Fay accepts. | The preview has one row: slot 2, `fay`. It does not contain `hana`. After the last accept, `mc missions show` has `ben` `ACCEPTED` and `fay` `ACCEPTED`. |
| AC7 | The demo shows a forbidden action with the role and the rule (DESIGN req 7). | Ava (CREW) runs `mc missions invite`. The step exits 1 in the script and the output has `CREW` and `Only directors and leads manage and view missions`. The script continues. |
| AC8 | The demo shows a cross-org check (DESIGN req 22). | Nick (lead of the other org) runs `mc missions show <Demo Survey id>`. The output has `Not found`. The script continues. |
| AC9 | An E2E test runs the script (DESIGN req 21). | The test starts uvicorn on a free port. It runs `scripts/demo.sh` with `MC_API_URL` and `MC_CONFIG_DIR` set. It asserts exit 0 and the key lines of AC2 to AC8. The test fails if the script exits non-zero. |
| AC10 | The script does not change the token of the user. | The script sets `MC_CONFIG_DIR` to a temporary folder, unless the caller already set it. The user token file is not changed. |
| AC11 | The README has a "Demo" section (DESIGN req 1, 2). | The section has the run command, the prerequisite (API running) and the warning that the script deletes all data. It has the real output of the script. |
| AC12 | The README has a "Test results" section (DESIGN req 2). | The section has the date, the commit hash, the command `uv run pytest` and its summary line (passed, failed, skipped). The numbers match a real run. |
| AC13 | The README has a "Known gaps" section for the P1 deferral. | The section lists start, complete and cancel (step 8), and the org-wide crew and mission view (step 10, requirement 11). |
| AC14 | `design/DESIGN.md` records the deferral. | Requirement 11 and build steps 8 and 10 are in the P1 list. The build order keeps the numbers 1 to 11 and marks steps 8 and 10 "Deferred to P1". Requirement 23 reads: the demo runs create, match, submit, approve, invite, accept and decline, and a crew member manages the own profile. The "Changes" table has a new row with the date and the reason. |

## Non-goals

# Spec: readme-demo

## Goal
Add a scripted CLI demo and test results to the README (build step 11, `design/DESIGN.md:74`). The script `scripts/demo.sh` runs the `mc` CLI against the running API and shows the CLI output in the console. It shows the happy path of what the CLI does today: a crew profile, a mission to APPROVED, invites, accept and decline. This gives a reviewer evidence of verification (DESIGN req 2, 23).

## Precondition
Build step 7 (staffing) is finished and committed. It adds `mc missions invite` and `mc assignments list|accept|decline` (`.work/staffing/spec.md`, AC24 to AC26). The demo uses these commands.

## Acceptance criteria
The demo mission is "Demo Survey", 2027-03-01 to 2027-03-10. It has slot 1 Piloting level 3 and slot 2 Medicine level 3. The seed data has no booking or leave of ben or hana in these dates (`packages/api/src/mc_api/seed.py`). Ben and hana have the closest fit by the ranking at `design/DESIGN.md:398`. The profile step changes only the Geology level of ben and a leave in June 2027. Neither change affects the matcher result.

| ID | Criterion | The tests must prove |
|---|---|---|
| AC1 | `scripts/demo.sh` resets the data with `uv run mc-seed`, then runs the journey against the running API (DESIGN req 23). | The script exits 0 on a clean database. The console shows one heading line for each journey step, in order, and each `mc` command with its output. |
| AC2 | Ben manages the own profile (DESIGN req 12, 13). Ben shows the profile, sets Geology to level 3, and lists the skills. Ben adds leave from 2027-06-01 to 2027-06-03, lists it, and removes it. | The profile output has `ben`, `Ben Carter` and `Artemis Space Agency`. The skill list has Geology with level 3. The add output has `Added unavailability <id>`. The list has the entry with `HOLIDAY`. After the remove, the list does not have the id. |
| AC3 | Leo creates the mission, adds the two slots and runs the matcher preview in DRAFT (DESIGN req 17). | The preview output has slot 1 `ben` and slot 2 `hana`, and `2 of 2 slots filled`. |
| AC4 | Leo submits. Diana approves (DESIGN req 8, 9). | The submit output shows `APPROVAL_REQUIRED`. The approve output shows `APPROVED`. |
| AC5 | Leo invites ben to slot 1 and hana to slot 2 (DESIGN req 18). Ben accepts. Hana declines (DESIGN req 10, 14). | After the invites, the mission output has `ben` `INVITED` and `hana` `INVITED`. The accept output has `ACCEPTED`. The decline output has `DECLINED`. |
| AC6 | The README has a "Demo" section (DESIGN req 1, 2). | The section has the run command, the prerequisite (API running) and the warning that the script deletes all data. It has the real output of the script. |

**Spec:** /Users/janeshorst/Dev/mutinex-interview/.work/readme-demo/spec.md
**Verify:** verify:full = `.claude/hooks/verify.sh full`; verify:fast = `.claude/hooks/verify.sh fast`
**Contract:** Covers, Tests must prove, Files, Interfaces, Global Constraints and Checkpoint are binding. Report each change to them to the human. The implementer chooses the code.

## Global Constraints
- Precondition: build step 7 (staffing) is finished and committed on the branch. Check with `uv run mc missions invite --help` and `uv run mc assignments --help`. If a command is missing, stop and tell the human.
- Postgres must run: `docker compose up -d`. The API must run for the script.
- Happy path only. Add no failure handling, no 403 or 404 steps and no rematch.
- Add no test. Do not edit anything under `packages/`.
- Do not edit `BRIEF.md`.
- Read `design/DESIGN.md` before you change it. Change only the deferral of AC9.
- Do not change the API, the CLI, `mc_shared` or the seed data.
- Write the README text in Simplified Technical English.
- The demo mission is "Demo Survey", 2027-03-01 to 2027-03-10. Slot 1 is Piloting level 3. Slot 2 is Medicine level 3.
- No commit steps in this plan. `implement-plan` commits the slice.

## Review Focus
None. The spec limits the demo to the happy path (spec non-goals).

## Interfaces
The README shows this output format of `scripts/demo.sh`.

```
== <N>. <title> ==      one heading line for each journey step, N from 1
$ mc <arguments>          one line for each mc command, before its output
<output of the command>
```

The script reads `MC_API_URL`, `MC_CONFIG_DIR`, `DATABASE_URL` and `COLUMNS`. It sets `COLUMNS=200` if the caller did not set it, so tables do not wrap. If the caller sets no `MC_CONFIG_DIR`, the script uses a temporary folder, so it does not replace the token of the user.

| N | Title |
|---|---|
| 1 | `Reset the demo data` |
| 2 | `Crew profile (ben)` |
| 3 | `Create the mission and its slots (leo)` |
| 4 | `Matcher preview in DRAFT (leo)` |
| 5 | `Submit (leo) and approve (diana)` |
| 6 | `Invite, accept and decline` |

### Slice 1: One script shows the crew profile, the approval and the staffing

**Files:**
- Create: `scripts/demo.sh` (executable)
- Modify: `README.md`
- Modify: `design/DESIGN.md`

**Covers:** AC1, AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5, AC6, AC7, AC8, AC9

**Tests must prove:** No test is added (spec non-goal). The slice is proved by a real run and by manual checks. Examples:

- Manual: step 2 output has `ben`, `Ben Carter`, `Artemis Space Agency`, a Geology row with `3`, `Added unavailability <id>`, a row with that id and `HOLIDAY`. The last availability list has no row with that id.
- Manual: step 4 output has slot 1 `ben`, slot 2 `hana`, and `2 of 2 slots filled`.
- Manual: step 5 output has `APPROVAL_REQUIRED` and then `APPROVED`.
- Manual: step 6 output has `ben` `INVITED` and `hana` `INVITED` after the invites, then `ACCEPTED` and `DECLINED`.
- Manual: `grep -n "^## Demo" README.md` → one line. The section has the run command `bash scripts/demo.sh`, the prerequisite that the API runs, the warning that the script deletes all data, and the real output of the run.
- Manual: `grep -n "^## Test results" README.md` → one line. The section has the date, the commit hash from `git rev-parse --short HEAD`, the command `uv run pytest`, and the real summary line.
- Manual: `grep -n "^## Known gaps" README.md` → one line. The section names rematch after a decline, the 403 and 404 checks, start, complete and cancel, and the org-wide view for directors.
- Manual: in `design/DESIGN.md`, requirement 11 and steps 8 and 10 are in the P1 list. The build order still has steps 1 to 11, and steps 8 and 10 have the text "Deferred to P1". Requirement 23 reads: the demo runs create, match, submit, approve, invite, accept and decline, and a crew member manages the own profile. The "Changes" table has a new row dated 2026-10-11 with the reason.

**Steps**
1. Read `design/DESIGN.md` in full.
2. Create `scripts/demo.sh` with `set -euo pipefail`. Make it executable.
3. Set the defaults of the Interfaces section.
4. Add one helper that prints the `$ mc ...` line and runs the command. Add one helper that prints a heading line.
5. Add step 1: run `uv run mc-seed`.
6. Add step 2: as `ben`, run `mc login`, `mc profile show`, `mc skills list` (to read the Geology ID), `mc profile skills set <id> --level 3`, `mc profile skills list`, `mc profile availability add --from 2027-06-01 --to 2027-06-03 --reason HOLIDAY`, `mc profile availability list`, `mc profile availability remove <id>`, `mc profile availability list`.
7. Add step 3: as `leo`, run `mc login`, `mc skills list` (Piloting and Medicine IDs), `mc missions create --title "Demo Survey" --start 2027-03-01 --end 2027-03-10`, and two `mc missions slots add` commands.
8. Add step 4: `mc missions match <id>`.
9. Add step 5: `mc missions submit <id>`, then as `diana` `mc login` and `mc missions approve <id>`.
10. Add step 6: as `leo`, `mc login`, `mc missions invite <id> --slot 1 --crew ben`, `mc missions invite <id> --slot 2 --crew hana`. As `ben`, `mc login` and `mc assignments accept <id>`. As `hana`, `mc login` and `mc assignments decline <id>`.
11. Run `docker compose up -d`, `uv run alembic upgrade head`, and start the API: `uv run uvicorn mc_api.main:app`.
12. Run `bash scripts/demo.sh` and save the output. Expected: exit 0 and the lines of the examples above.
13. Run `uv run pytest -q` and save the summary line. If a test fails, stop and tell the human.
14. Add the README sections "Demo", "Test results" and "Known gaps". Paste the real output. Keep the README text in STE.
15. Edit `design/DESIGN.md` as in the last example above.
16. Stop the API.

**Checkpoint:** With the API running, `bash scripts/demo.sh` → exit 0 and the console shows the real CLI output of the six steps. Then `.claude/hooks/verify.sh full` → exit 0, no ERROR lines. Then `grep -c "^## \(Demo\|Test results\|Known gaps\)" README.md` → `3`.
